lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Dejair Caitano do Nascimento | Lesson 24 -- Bangkok Is Now

listenings.text: Hello, my name is Priya Raman. I am a neurologist from Chennai, in India. I work at a university hospital, and my field is pain medicine. My main focus is nerve pain in patients with diabetes. I have been in this field for about twelve years. This is my third time at this congress, and every year I meet colleagues from countries I have never visited. That is the part I like most. I am here for the workshop on Wednesday, and I hope to hear about new research from South America.

Good morning! Are you Doctor Caitano? I'm Mehmet, from Istanbul. I'm a pharmacologist, like you. I read your abstract last night, the one about leprosy and pain. I have to say, it's not my area, but it was really interesting. We work on chemotherapy and nerve pain, so maybe there is some common ground. Are you presenting today, or tomorrow? I'd like to see your poster, if you have time. And if you're free for lunch, some of us are going to the Thai place across the street.

extra_audio.text: Hi, I'm Dejair, from Brazil. I work on pain and leprosy. In a nutshell, the pain is not only about nerve damage. Our data strongly suggest that early treatment helps. If you send me your protocol, I'll share our data. It was great meeting you. Let's stay in touch.

reading.rtitle: After the Course: Keeping Your English Alive
paras: The end of a course is not the end of learning. Many adult learners make a lot of progress in a few months, and then lose some of it in the year after. The reason is simple: English that you do not use gets slower. The good news is that it also comes back fast.

Researchers who keep their spoken English alive usually have a small, regular routine. They listen to one podcast or one talk a week, often with an accent that is still hard for them. They speak for a few minutes every week, with a colleague, a teacher or even alone, and they record themselves. And they use every congress as a chance to practice, not as a test.

The most important part is the next step. After a big event, write down one conversation that went well and one moment that was difficult. That is your new plan. A congress is a milestone, not a finish line: what you build after it decides your next level.
reading.source: Written for this class from common advice for adult language learners.
